# Apple Human Interface Guidelines

Use the relevant Apple guidance to make concrete design decisions. This package
contains a router, 13 family routes, 158 operational topic skills, and supporting
article-level references. It is
independent of Apple. The sources are a dated English HIG snapshot; check the
official source when a task depends on a newer release or a disputed detail.

## Route the task

1. Identify the target platform, device context, and user task from the request or
   project. Ask for the platform only when it materially affects the answer and
   cannot be inferred. Preserve the user's framework and product requirements.
2. Select the relevant family below and read that family's `SKILL.md`. Follow its
   link to the exact topic procedure under `.topics/` and read that `SKILL.md`.
   Apply its decision procedure, then consult its supporting article for facts
   and platform qualifications. Topic skills are explicitly read by installed
   file path; automatic nested discovery is not required.
   For platform support, product feasibility, or platform adaptation, first read each relevant
   platform's Getting started procedure, then the specific component or technology
   procedure. Check both the platform model and the surface's support limits.
3. Before finalizing the route, search the [complete topic index](references/topic-index.md)
   for the task's concepts as well as component or framework names. Its trigger
   descriptions connect everyday product requests to Apple's topic names; users
   need not name an Apple framework. Read the owning family and matching topic
   procedure before its supporting reference. Search relevant rows instead of
   loading the full corpus for a narrow question.
   For a screenshot-specific or animated example, also consult its
   [original visual explanation](references/media/index.md) when available.
4. Apply shared guidance and the target platform's documented differences. A
   missing platform subsection means no additional rule is stated; it does not
   prove support, nonapplicability, or identical behavior across platforms.
5. Compose families when the task crosses them: a component can also require
   accessibility, typography, localization, input, or system-experience guidance.
   Map the brief's material decisions to their owning topics. Read the owning
   procedure for each explicit concern, such as privacy or accessibility, as well
   as the affected components; a neighboring procedure's reminder is insufficient.
   Use [platform and task routes](references/platforms-and-tasks.md) when useful.
   In a review, map each supplied control to its candidate component procedure
   even when markup or behavior is missing. Use it to frame inspection questions;
   missing evidence neither proves a defect nor removes that control from scope.

All paths are relative to **this installed package**, not the shell's current
directory. No Python, network, sibling skill installation, or authoring cache is
required to read the guidance.

## Perform the requested work

Inspect the supplied brief, flow, code, specification or image before deciding
what is wrong or choosing a framework. Use the user's requested mode:

- **Design:** produce an implementable specification or interaction/state model
  from the topic's decision procedure, with concrete transitions and acceptance
  checks. Connect choices to the user's task and target platform.
- **Implement:** prefer the project's native system components when they supply
  the needed behavior. HIG explains experience requirements; verify API names,
  availability, and code against the appropriate SDK documentation. Make the
  authorized changes in the existing stack; a prose explanation alone does not
  complete an implementation request.
- **Review:** describe the observed problem, its effect, the relevant HIG rule,
  and a concrete correction. Separate source-backed findings from your own
  suggested improvements. Do not invent violations without inspecting evidence.
- **Adapt:** preserve the product task, data and useful state while applying the
  destination platform's interaction model. Patch the supplied artifact or give
  an explicit before/after contract when a design specification is requested.

Topic procedures are framework agnostic. Their worked examples and pseudocode
teach decisions, not a requirement to replace the project's technology. Load
related procedures only for a decision that actually depends on them.

Complete the topic's observable checks and report passed, failed and not executed
separately. Reading a file, citing Apple, or proposing a test does not establish
runtime behavior. Static code or screenshots cannot prove assistive-technology
order, native rendering, physical comfort, haptics, or SDK compilation.

Include official article/section links for material recommendations. Preserve
qualifications such as “consider,” “prefer,” and “avoid”; do not turn design
advice into invented universal requirements. Retain units and platform scope for
numerical specifications. If source passages conflict, describe the conflict
and the conservative application rather than silently changing the source.

## Source boundaries

This is comprehensive local guidance, not a verbatim Apple manual or an SDK API
reference. Original media explanations are supplementary to article references;
the source page remains useful for visual demonstrations. Source snapshots and
review status live in the repository's coverage report, outside ordinary skill
loading. Do not infer that a source has been independently reviewed just because
its local file exists.

Historical `navigation-bars` links now resolve to current Toolbars guidance;
`in-app-purchase` resolves to Apple In-App Purchase. The old Touch Bar and Messages
for Business HIG pages were unavailable at this snapshot. Do not fabricate their
current rules. Translations, archived pages, and complete linked SDK/WWDC libraries
are outside the source boundary.

name: apple-hig-designing-for-macos
description: Use when creating, reviewing, or adapting a Mac experience for multiple windows, menu commands, keyboard workflows, precise selection, or desktop file work.

# Give desktop work desktop control

Read [Designing for macOS](../../references/designing-for-macos.md). Inspect the current task, document/content model, windows, commands, and interruption behavior. Determine whether the request is a design, review, or port. Preserve the existing stack and distinguish observed behavior from proposals or missing runtime evidence.

Choose window boundaries around useful units of work. If documents or parallel comparisons benefit from independent windows, retain their own selections and edits. If one workspace suffices, make it resizable and avoid unnecessary modal navigation. Plan full screen for focused work without making it the only usable arrangement. Keep essential commands reachable even when a window is partly offscreen.

Build a command inventory from the task. Put app commands in the menu bar, give common operations appropriate shortcuts, and ensure a keyboard-only completion path. Align toolbar/contextual controls with those same actions and availability states. Use pointer precision for selection and editing rather than inflating a phone-style interface across the display. Preserve conventional file opening/saving and relevant Dock-menu behavior.

Specify app activation changes: switching away and back must preserve work and clearly distinguish the active target for commands. Offer customization where different work styles justify it, such as tools or window arrangement; do not require customization before basic use.

**Before → decision → after:** A photo catalog port displays every album as a full-screen drill-down and exposes Export only through a floating touch menu. Desktop comparison needs persistent context and a discoverable command. After, an album sidebar and resizable detail area support selection; File > Export and a keyboard command act on that selection, and optional second windows compare collections without losing the original state.

Deliver the revised window/command model or implementation, with a keyboard path and activation scenario. Fail if menu and toolbar act on different selections, switching apps loses edits, or resizing hides the only completion action. Linux inspection does not establish actual menu-bar integration, multi-display behavior, or native keyboard accessibility.

Use [Keyboards](../../../apple-hig-inputs/.topics/apple-hig-keyboards/SKILL.md) for command details, [Layout](../../../apple-hig-foundations/.topics/apple-hig-layout/SKILL.md) for window constraints, and [Mac Catalyst](../../../apple-hig-technologies/.topics/apple-hig-mac-catalyst/SKILL.md) when adapting an iPad app through that technology.

# Preserve context without multiplying clutter

Read [the window guide](../../references/windows.md). This workflow is application advice for the supported multiwindow platforms, not a claim that every OS has identical windows.

Inspect document/task identity, current windows, parallel-work needs, size ranges, platform, and create/review/adapt request. Distinguish a primary workspace from a short auxiliary task and a context-following panel. Record open/reuse/close behavior and main/key ownership from evidence; a screenshot does not establish window identity.

Open another window when preserving context or parallel work helps, with explicit Open in New Window where useful; avoid clutter by default. Retain system frames/movement/resize/close controls and call them windows in product copy. Set useful size constraints and adapt between them. On iPad protect leading tools from window controls and support the chosen fullscreen/windowed context. # Make the task accessible

Read [Accessibility guidance](../../references/accessibility.md) before applying platform values. This procedure turns that guidance into task-level changes; its artifact format and prioritization are application engineering advice, not additional Apple requirements.

## Establish what can be evaluated

Identify the supported platform, the person's task from entry to completion, and whether the request is design, review, or adaptation. Inspect the supplied screens, content, interaction description, semantics, or implementation. Record which evidence exists: a screenshot can establish visible labels and geometry, but cannot establish spoken names, focus order, alternative activation, or preference behavior. Continue using explicit assumptions when the platform or behavior is missing; ask only when the choice changes the requested result.

For a review, connect each finding to an observed barrier and its consequence for that task. Separate untested behavior needing verification from confirmed defects. For a design or adaptation, change the authorized artifact itself: a revised screen specification, interaction contract, or implementation. A general accessibility checklist alone is not the deliverable.

## Remove the barriers that the task contains

Trace the task without assuming sight, hearing, fine motor control, speech, or fast responses. Select the applicable branches:

- **Reading and visual distinctions:** Preserve content and available actions when text enlarges. Use the guide's platform-specific text defaults and minima; its resizing guidance is at least 200%, with 140% stated for watchOS. Reflow or expose another usable arrangement rather than clipping essential labels. Pair color distinctions with text, shape, or symbols. Evaluate actual foreground/background combinations in light and dark appearances; use a contrast calculator and preserve the guide's stated contrast-table scope instead of claiming that its values alone establish conformance. If the default scheme falls short, specify the Increase Contrast treatment.
- **Information carried by sound or imagery:** Identify what information would disappear when sound or sight is unavailable. Choose captions for synchronized audible events, subtitles for dialogue translation, audio description for visual events, or transcripts for a complete text account according to the content. Specify descriptions for meaningful interface/content imagery and omit redundant decoration. Pair essential sound feedback with a perceivable visual or appropriate haptic equivalent.
- **Manipulation and navigation:** Distinguish visible control size from its actual activation area and separation. Use the guide's platform default as the starting point; its smaller minimum is not a blanket recommendation for dense controls. Replace essential complex or repeated gestures with a labeled onscreen action. Make the complete task navigable and activatable with the supported keyboard and assistive input paths; speech must not be necessary. Preserve system accessibility shortcuts. For custom controls, specify names, roles, values, states, and task order rather than assuming their appearance supplies semantics.
- **Time, motion, and comprehension:** Give people time to read and act; prefer explicit dismissal when transient content requires attention. If motion is present, define a Reduce Motion version that retains state and meaning while reducing automatic movement, bounce, zoom, or depth changes. If media autoplays, provide playback control and consider a global preference; honor Dim Flashing Lights where applicable. Keep the task's navigation and wording consistent rather than adding instructional clutter.

Apply the relevant platform condition. For Assistive Access on iOS/iPadOS, focus on core tasks with one interaction per screen and the source's two confirmations for difficult-to-reverse actions in that mode. For visionOS, keep controls in comfortable view, avoid head-locked content and repeated large gestures, and accommodate hand/head Pointer Control and Zoom. These conditions do not apply automatically to every platform.

## Deliver and check the result

Return the revised artifact or evidence-based review, including the barrier, the concrete change, and its acceptance check. State which platform/preferences were considered and which claims remain unverified. Prioritize blockers to completing the task over cosmetic refinements.

Exercise each selected alternative along the same entry-to-completion path. Fail the check if essential content or actions disappear at the specified text scale, information remains available through only one sense, a required gesture has no equivalent, focus cannot reach/activate a necessary control, or a requested motion accommodation removes meaning. Measure contrast and activation geometry when the evidence permits; report missing measurements rather than inventing them. Use Accessibility Inspector and relevant VoiceOver, Switch Control, Full Keyboard Access, AssistiveTouch, or Pointer Control tests on supported Apple environments. Static inspection or a Linux run cannot establish those runtime results, Apple-device comfort, or App Store Accessibility Nutrition Label eligibility.

## Worked transformation

**Before:** An iPad astronomy log marks observation quality only with green/red dots, announces saving with a chime, and exposes Delete only by a two-finger gesture.

**Decision:** Logging must remain understandable without color or sound and operable without that gesture. Retain compact rows while making status and actions explicit.

**After:** Each row reads “Clear” or “Clouded” alongside its symbol; saving exposes a persistent “Saved” state; a labeled row action opens Delete. The screen specification includes expanded-text reflow, semantic row status, and keyboard/assistive activation acceptance checks. These are proposed changes until the actual implementation passes those checks; the specification does not claim VoiceOver was tested.

## Continue only where needed

For detailed spoken structure and rotor navigation, use [VoiceOver](../../../apple-hig-technologies/.topics/apple-hig-voiceover/SKILL.md). On Mac with autosave off identify unsaved work and request saving at consequential exits; apply dirty/Edited cues according to the source rather than all at once. Let people choose name/format/location and preserve extension preferences. Use Quick Look for useful previews rather than forcing app switches. Prefer system text styles and runtime font APIs so optical design/tracking adapt to size. If a custom face is needed, verify weight/legibility and provide equivalent text-size and Bold Text behavior; thin faces may need more size than the table suggests. Use loose leading for sustained/wide reading, avoiding tight leading across three or more lines.

Decide how content expands. Grow containers, permit labels to wrap, stack timestamps/glyphs, and reduce columns rather than aggressively truncating essential reading. Preserve context and finish eligible user-initiated input-free tasks before suspension. Notify only for important completion requiring another timely step; routine results can appear on return. # Windows Source: [Apple Human Interface Guidelines](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/windows) Snapshot: 2026-10-25. Original implementation guidance derived from the source. Primary windows host app navigation, content, and actions. Auxiliary windows focus on one task or area and typically close after that task. iPadOS, macOS, and visionOS windows establish content boundaries and enable multitasking with system movement, sizing, and closing controls. ## Best practices Adapt smoothly to size changes. Open new windows when preserving context or working in parallel helps, without generating clutter by default. Offer Open in New Window in a context or File menu when useful. Retain system frames and controls instead of imitating them. Call the experience a window in user-facing copy; scene is an implementation term. ## Platform considerations This multiwindow component guidance marks iOS, tvOS, and watchOS unsupported. ### iPadOS People choose fullscreen or windowed behavior in Multitasking & Gestures settings. Fullscreen fills the display and uses app switching; windowed mode supports multiple resizable, movable windows with remembered placement. Move leading toolbar items inward when window controls appear so they do not overlap. Consider gestures to open content in a new window, such as expanding a collection item with a pinch. Quick Look can present a single file without a custom window if the app supports multiple windows. ### macOS Support normal movement, resize, minimization, and frequent switching among multiple apps' windows. Games also need the appropriate system game-window configuration. #### macOS window anatomy A frame above the body supplies movement, window controls, and optionally a toolbar. Edges normally resize. A rare bottom bar is also part of the frame. #### macOS window states An app has one main window; the system has one key/input window at a time. A floating panel can be key while its document stays main. Dock activation brings app windows forward but makes only the recently used one key. Other windows are inactive. Colored close/minimize/zoom controls identify key state; inactive and non-key main windows use gray, and inactive windows lose vibrancy. Some panels take key status only through the title bar or keyboard-input controls. Custom rendering must preserve these automatic state cues. Avoid critical controls at the bottom, which may be offscreen; reserve bottom bars for small contextual summaries, using an inspector for more detail. ### visionOS Windows and volumetric windows can each contain 2D/3D content and coexist in Shared or Full Space. Plain style omits the glass plane. The system positions the first opened surface, then people can move it. #### visionOS windows Default windows use an upright glass plane with close, move, and resize controls, and can add Share, tabs, toolbars, and ornaments. Dynamic scale preserves apparent size across distance. Prefer familiar windows for familiar tasks, reserving immersion for meaningful content. Retain the glass background: it adapts to surroundings and communicates scale and position; removing it weakens legibility and grouping, while an opaque replacement conceals surroundings. Default initial size is 1280×720 pt, placed about 2 meters ahead with an apparent width of about 3 meters. Avoid excess empty space and choose a shape suited to content. Set minimum/maximum sizes and adapt layout throughout. Keep 3D depth shallow in a window because content too far from its surface is clipped; use a volume for deeper objects. #### visionOS volumes Volumes show bounded content from multiple angles; close and move controls turn to face the viewer. Prefer them for rich 3D scenes over UI-centric interfaces. Pin 2D overlays to 3D content with attachments and test multiple viewpoints. Dynamic scaling usually improves distant legibility and interaction, but fixed scaling (the default) suits true-to-life products. From visionOS 2, a baseplate border glow on look reveals bounds and resize controls when content does not fill them. Full-bleed content or a custom baseplate may not need it. Volumes can have an ornament alongside toolbar/tabs: use attachment anchors to keep its position viewer-relative, place it on another edge, and usually add only one. Choose a floor-parallel alignment for largely viewed objects, or a viewer-tilting alignment when interactive content should remain usable while reclining. ## Resources Official implementation links and revision metadata follow. #### Related [Layout](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/layout) [Split views](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/split-views) [Multitasking](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/multitasking) #### Developer documentation — SwiftUI — SwiftUI — UIKit — AppKit #### Videos ## Change log Revision dates recorded by Apple: June 9, 2025, June 10, 2024, June 21, 2023.

# File management Source: [Apple Human Interface Guidelines](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/file-management) Snapshot: 2026-10-25. Document apps should work with the filesystem people already use: Finder on Mac and Files on iPhone, iPad, and Apple Vision Pro. tvOS/watchOS do not normally provide document browsing. ## Creating and opening files Provide standard New/Open commands and keyboard shortcuts on Mac/iPad. Expose a discoverable Add action; Mac creation also belongs in File. A custom browser may initially emphasize a relevant folder or recent location but should still let people browse the wider filesystem. ## Saving work Autosave periodically and when closing or leaving the app so work survives unless explicitly canceled or deleted. Hide extensions initially, let people show them, and honor that choice consistently across Open/Save UI. ## Quick Look previews Preview unsupported attachments without forcing a context switch through a Quick Look viewer. If producing a custom type, supply a generator so Finder, Files, Spotlight, and other apps can preview it. Depending on file type, previews may support audio, markup, or 3D inspection. ## Platform considerations No additional tvOS, visionOS, or watchOS rules are specified. ### iOS, iPadOS #### Document launcher From iOS/iPadOS 18, a system launcher combines a title card with two app actions, a customizable background/accessories, and a file-browser sheet with optional app tools. Assign primary/secondary actions to important work, usually creation plus a template or additional choice. Keep backgrounds distinct and quiet. Accessories may layer around the title for depth but must not obscure name/actions; test all sizes and orientations. Animate sparingly with gentle motion that supports content. #### File provider app extension An extension can expose import/export/open/move access to other apps. Filter open/import results to the host's accepted types and show useful metadata or local/remote status. Allow a destination choice for export/move unless there is only one directory; new subdirectories can help. Avoid a second top toolbar because the host modal already supplies one. Apps can also browse other providers through standard document-browser support. ### macOS #### Custom file management Prefer the standard browser. A justified custom opener should support useful recents, filters, and multiselection; adapt Open to the task, such as Insert. Let people change name, format, and location during saving, with logical initial folders and an initially Untitled document. Add a Save accessory view only for useful related options. #### Finder Sync extensions For local/remote synchronization, Finder Sync can add item status badges, contextual management commands, and global toolbar actions. Respect disabled autosaving: identify unsaved content and request saving on close, quit, logout, or restart. Show dirty dots on the close control and Window-menu name only when autosave is off. An Edited title suffix can apply in either mode but must disappear after an automatic or explicit save. ## Resources Official implementation links and revision metadata follow. #### Related [Toolbars](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/toolbars) [File menu](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/the-menu-bar#File-menu) [Printing](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/printing) #### Developer documentation — SwiftUI #### Videos ## Change log Revision dates recorded by Apple: June 10, 2024, June 21, 2023.

App-wide configuration, task-local controls, and system Settings belong in different places according to how often and where people need them. ## Best practices Optimize defaults for most people and automatically detect capabilities such as connected controllers or appearance. Keep the settings set small. Support expected access, including Command-Comma and game Escape. Use predictable relationships among content and controls while adapting to the actual available space. ## Visual hierarchy Prioritize important content toward the top and leading edge in reading order. Use system components for RTL adaptation. Align related items, indent subordinate items, and group relationships with space, containers, or separators. Reveal secondary choices progressively through disclosure, menus, nested views, or scrollable media sections. Distinguish navigation/controls with Liquid Glass and scroll-edge treatments; extend full-window backgrounds under bars and sidebars. A background extension effect can mirror and blur imagery under adjacent components instead of hiding essential original art. ## Adaptability Handle size classes, display sizes, orientation/aspect ratio, Dynamic Island, external displays, Display Zoom, resizable windows, text changes, localized length/direction/fonts, and date/number formats. Use SwiftUI or Auto Layout, safe areas, margins, and layout modifiers. Orientation-locked games must still resize. With large text, stack horizontal content, increase row height, and allow wrapping. Apple’s Unity accessibility plug-in can supply Dynamic Type in games. Preview smallest/largest layouts first, then multiple devices, localizations, sizes, iPad resizing, and iPhone Mirroring. Scale backgrounds to fill without distorting aspect ratio; extreme wide/short or narrow/tall windows may crop much more than standard displays. ### Size classes Each axis is compact or regular, describing available width or height rather than device type or orientation. All four combinations can occur as apps resize, multitask, or mirror. Base layout on these environmental values, not idiom/orientation guesses. Preserve functionality across classes while changing how much is exposed, such as sidebar versus tabs or visible actions versus overflow. The platform idiom remains the same during resizing, so preserve its familiar character. ## Guides and safe areas Layout guides supply rectangular regions for alignment, spacing, margins, and readable text widths; custom guides can add app-specific structure. Safe areas exclude edge obstructions such as camera hardware, status bars, tab bars, and toolbars. Keep important content and controls within the appropriate safe regions. ## Platform considerations No extra iOS/iPadOS rules are listed. ### macOS Do not rely on the bottom of a window for essential controls because it may sit below the physical display. Avoid placing content behind the top camera housing. ### tvOS Inset primary content 60 pt vertically and 80 pt horizontally to withstand TV overscan/settings. Leave enough focus padding for system enlargement so focused items do not obscure important information. #### Grids Use consistent row/column spacing, sufficient room for enlargement, and symmetrical partial items at both horizontal edges. Add extra separation above and below row titles. UIKit collection flow layout derives the column count from item width and spacing. Set minimum/maximum bounds only to avoid overlaps or unwieldy layouts, not to disable resizing. Use inline 3D content sparingly for meaningful additions; inset it so it avoids controls and window edges. Prefer volumes or immersive spaces for large/model-centric content. Preserve the table’s stated scope rather than assuming it replaces a separate conformance evaluation. If default colors fall short, Increase Contrast must supply a higher-contrast scheme. Test both light and dark. Prefer semantic system colors that adapt to accessibility preferences. Pair color with shape, icons, or text; red/green and blue/orange distinctions can be difficult. Let people customize chart or character colors where useful. Give VoiceOver meaningful descriptions of interface and content. ## Hearing Make dialogue and important information available without sound. Captions describe audible information in synchrony with media, subtitles present dialogue in a chosen language, audio descriptions narrate otherwise visual events in audio pauses, and transcripts provide a complete text account of audible and visual information. Let people adjust text presentation. Pair sound feedback with matching haptics and visual direction cues, especially for offscreen game or spatial events. Music Haptics and audio graphs on iOS/iPadOS can offer tactile representations of music and data. ## Mobility Use comfortable controls and sufficient separation, not just adequate visible size. |Platform|Default control|Minimum control| |---|---:|---:| |iOS, iPadOS|44 × 44 pt|28 × 28 pt| |macOS|28 × 28 pt|20 × 20 pt| |tvOS|66 × 66 pt|56 × 56 pt| |visionOS|60 × 60 pt|28 × 28 pt| |watchOS|44 × 44 pt|28 × 28 pt| The source suggests around 12 pt padding for bezelled elements and 24 pt outside visible edges for elements without a bezel. Use simple gestures for repeated tasks and offer an onscreen alternative for essential gestures, such as a dismiss button alongside swipe-to-dismiss. Avoid requiring complex multiple-finger or multiple-hand actions. Label controls so Voice Control can target them. Siri/Shortcuts can expose repeated tasks through voice, Action buttons, Home Screen, and Control Center. Test VoiceOver, AssistiveTouch, Full Keyboard Access, Pointer Control, and Switch Control rather than assuming support. ## Speech Support complete keyboard navigation and Full Keyboard Access; preserve system accessibility shortcuts. Support Switch Control navigation and activation through hardware, controller, and sound inputs such as a click or pop, so speech is never a necessary input method. ## Cognitive Use familiar, simple, consistent navigation and gestures. Prefer explicit dismissal over timed disappearance, allowing time for processing and assistive navigation. Games can offer difficulty, reaction-time, success-criteria, and control-assistance accommodations. Give clear playback controls and consider a global autoplay preference. Respect Dim Flashing Lights during media playback. Honor Reduce Motion by reducing automatic and repeated movement, scaling, zooming, and peripheral effects. Reduce spring bounce; tie appropriate motion directly to gestures; avoid animated depth changes and blur transitions; replace spatial translations with fades. Fast or blinking motion can distract, cause dizziness, or trigger seizures. Keep controls inside a comfortable field of view; horizontal arrangements usually strain the neck less than tall ones. Avoid rapid shifts of attention among distant locations. Reduce peripheral animation speed and intensity, use gentle camera/video motion, and avoid making the surrounding world move without the person’s control. # Multitasking Source: [Apple Human Interface Guidelines](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/multitasking) Snapshot: 2026-10-25. Original implementation guidance derived from the source. Support switching and simultaneous work wherever the platform allows it; exceptions include some games and a visionOS Full Space. Be ready to preserve context whenever focus changes. ## Best practices Pause attention-dependent gameplay/media when leaving the experience, with seamless resumption. Distinguish audio interruption types: sustained primary audio such as music/podcasts requires an indefinite pause, while brief directions may duck or pause temporarily and then restore. Finish input-free user-initiated tasks in the background before suspension. Notify only for important/time-sensitive completion that prompts another step; routine background work can report status on return. ## Platform considerations This multitasking mode is unsupported in watchOS. ### iOS Picture in Picture allows video/FaceTime beside another app. ### iPadOS Support several apps' windows and multiple windows of one app. Fullscreen windows switch through the app switcher; windowed mode allows resize, placement, tiling, fullscreen, minimize, and close. Frontmost colored controls/shadows communicate state. PiP can overlay either mode. Apps neither control nor receive the person's multitasking configuration, so adapt to size rather than assuming one layout. ### macOS Multiple apps/windows are the normal environment. Preserve system layering and main/key/inactive appearance cues. ### tvOS Supported experiences can browse/play while another movie/show remains in PiP. ### visionOS Shared Space hosts multiple windows/volumes with one active window. Looking elsewhere activates that window and lets the prior window recede/translucently dim. Preserve system feathered-edge feedback instead of changing edges. Closing a window backgrounds rather than quits the app; closing a Now Playing window pauses audio, which can resume in Control Center. Video started in one window should continue when the person merely looks at another, qualifying the general attention-pause rule. Non-Now-Playing audio can duck when attention shifts. ## Resources Official implementation links and revision metadata follow. #### Related [Layout](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/layout) [Windows](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/windows) [Playing video](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/playing-video) #### Developer documentation — UIKit — UIKit #### Videos ## Change log Revision dates recorded by Apple: June 9, 2025, December 5, 2023, June 21, 2023.

# The menu bar Source: [Apple Human Interface Guidelines](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/the-menu-bar) Snapshot: 2026-10-25. Original implementation guidance derived from the source. ## Contents - [Anatomy](#Anatomy) - [Best practices](#Best-practices) - [App menu](#App-menu) - [File menu](#File-menu) - [Edit menu](#Edit-menu) - [Format menu](#Format-menu) - [View menu](#View-menu) - [App-specific menus](#App-specific-menus) - [Window menu](#Window-menu) - [Help menu](#Help-menu) - [Dynamic menu items](#Dynamic-menu-items) - [Platform considerations](#Platform-considerations) The menu bar exposes an app's full command structure on Mac and iPad. Familiar ordering and keyboard equivalents let people discover capabilities and work with a hardware keyboard. ## Anatomy Order supported menus as app name, File, Edit, Format, View, app-specific menus, Window, Help. Mac additionally places Apple at the leading end and menu-bar extras at the trailing end. ## Best practices Preserve standard menus, order, and shortcuts. Keep unavailable commands visible but disabled. Use familiar action glyphs and brief, preferably one-word menu titles; multiword titles use title case. Standard controls often provide command enablement automatically. ## App menu This menu holds app-wide rather than document/window tasks. Use the short app name, preferably 16 characters or fewer, without a version. Standard order is About (alone before a separator), Settings…, custom configuration items in the same group, Services, Hide App, Hide Others, Show All, and Quit App. Services and hide/show commands are Mac-only, and iPad has further differences below. Settings is for app-level configuration; document-specific settings belong in File. Hide App activates the previous app; Show All restores others behind it. Option can change Quit to Quit and Keep Windows. ## File menu Omit or rename File when the app handles no files. Preserve the following functional order where relevant: | Command | Behavior and qualification | | --- | --- | | New Item | Create a document/file/window; name the actual kind of item | | Open / Open… | Open selection directly or request a selection, adding ellipsis for the latter | | Open Recent | Recognizable names, newest first, usually with Clear Menu; avoid full paths | | Close | Close current window/document; Option offers Close All | | Close Tab | Replaces Close in tabbed windows; Option offers Close Other Tabs; consider separate Close Window | | Close File | Close all views of one file when several views can coexist | | Save | Save current content; autosave periodically; ask a new file's name/location and offer formats in the Save sheet | | Save All | Save every open document | | Duplicate | Keep original and copy open; Option offers Save As; clearer than ambiguous copy/save-to commands | | Rename… / Move To… | Change current name or request another location | | Export As… | Choose name, location, and atypical format; retain the original open and do not open the export | | Revert To | With autosave, expose recent versions and version browser; selected version replaces current content | | Page Setup… | Document-specific paper size/orientation; retain parameters with the document | | Print… | Standard printer/fax/PDF output; printer choice and frequently changed copy counts belong here rather than Page Setup | ## Edit menu Keep Edit useful for any editable content, including nondocument apps. File/object search may belong in File rather than Edit. Order Undo and Redo, Cut/Copy/Paste/Paste and Match Style/Delete/Select All, then Find, Spelling and Grammar, Substitutions, Transformations, Speech, Start Dictation, Emoji & Symbols. Name undo/redo targets, such as Typing or the command reversed. Cut removes to Clipboard; Copy duplicates there; Paste leaves Clipboard reusable; Paste and Match Style adopts surrounding formatting; Delete removes without copying and should be named Delete rather than Erase/Clear. Select All covers the current document/text container. Find normally includes Find, Find and Replace, next/previous, use selection, and jump to selection. Spelling/grammar includes its panel, immediate check, while-typing spelling, grammar, and autocorrection. Substitutions includes its panel plus smart copy/paste, quotes, dashes, links, data detection, and replacement. Transformations offers uppercase/lowercase/capitalization. Speech starts/stops spoken selected text. The system adds dictation and the character viewer at the bottom. ## Format menu Omit Format when rich-text editing is absent. Font comes before Text. Font includes the font panel, bold/italic/underline, bigger/smaller, colors, and copy/paste style. Text includes left/center/justified/right alignment, writing direction, ruler, and copy/paste ruler. ## View menu View controls appearance rather than managing individual windows. Include it even for only a supported subset, such as fullscreen. Show/hide labels must reflect the next action. Standard order covers tab bar visibility, tab overview, toolbar visibility, toolbar customization, sidebar visibility, then Enter/Exit Full Screen. ## App-specific menus Put custom menus between View and Window and expose custom commands there even when advanced or available elsewhere. This supports discovery, keyboard shortcuts, and Full Keyboard Access. Order around the app's hierarchy and common usage; for example, containers precede objects and object formatting. The source's wording about general versus specialized ordering is internally inconsistent, so use the concrete hierarchy and frequency criteria rather than inventing an absolute rule. ## Window menu Provide it even for a single-window app so Minimize and Zoom remain keyboard-accessible. It manages windows; View customizes appearance and File closes them. Panel show/hide commands can live here, except font/color panels already in Format. Standard order: | Command | Behavior | | --- | --- | | Minimize | Active window to Dock; Option offers Minimize All | | Zoom | Toggle content-appropriate size and user size; Option offers Zoom All; distinct from fullscreen | | Show Previous/Next Tab | Navigate document tabs | | Move Tab to New Window | Detach current tab | | Merge All Windows | Combine into one tabbed window | | Enter/Exit Full Screen | Include here only without a View menu; retain Minimize and Zoom separately | | Bring All to Front | Preserve positions, sizes, and layering; Option offers neatly tiled Arrange in Front | | Open window names | Alphabetical window list; omit panels and modal views | ## Help menu Keep Help at the trailing end. Help Book content adds system search and opens in Help Viewer. Standard entries can include feedback to Apple and App Help. Separate additional items such as registration or release notes from primary documentation, and keep their number low or link them from the documentation instead. ## Dynamic menu items Modifier-dependent alternates can accelerate advanced actions, such as Option-Minimize All. They must have discoverable alternatives because they are hidden by default. Prefer menu-bar use over Dock/context menus, require only one modifier, and let system menu sizing account for the widest alternate. ## Platform considerations The menu bar is unsupported in iOS, tvOS, visionOS, and watchOS. ### iPadOS The bar is hidden until a top-edge pointer movement or downward swipe and occupies the status-bar area. It centers horizontally; Mac aligns leading and is visible by default. iPad has no Apple menu or extras, and fullscreen window controls appear within the bar. About, Services, and app-visibility items are unavailable on iPad. Every function must also be reachable through app UI because the bar is often hidden; dynamic commands additionally require a hardware keyboard. Reserve App > Settings for the app's page in system Settings; link in-app preferences and other custom app-wide configuration beneath it in that group. Consider listing navigation tabs in View with shortcuts. Taller touch-friendly rows may justify submenus more often than on Mac. ### macOS The system Apple menu stays first and cannot be changed. Extras occupy trailing space when available. Space pressure can reduce intermenu spacing and truncate titles. Fullscreen generally hides the bar until the pointer reaches the top. #### Menu bar extras An extra remains available while the app runs even when it is not frontmost, but the system can hide it to protect menu space. Use a black/transparent template icon or SF Symbol so system tint adapts to background and selection; menu-bar height is 24 pt. Prefer a menu over a popover unless the feature is too complex for one. Let people choose whether to add the extra, optionally offering that choice during setup. Never rely on its visibility or fixed position; provide another route such as a Dock menu. ## Resources Official implementation links and revision metadata follow. #### Related [Menus](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/menus) [Dock menus](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/dock-menus) [Standard keyboard shortcuts](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/keyboards#Standard-keyboard-shortcuts) #### Developer documentation — SwiftUI — UIKit — AppKit #### Videos ## Change log Revision dates recorded by Apple: June 9, 2025.

# Architecture notes — macOS window specification

This specification replaces the shared hidden buffer and fixed window model. It defines intended behavior; no application implementation or native execution is supplied. Preserve the existing technology stack.

## Document and window identity

- Each architecture-note document owns a stable document ID, optional file identity/location, editable content, revision counter, persisted revision and save operation. Each new Untitled note receives a distinct ID and recoverable draft location immediately.
- Each primary window owns a window ID, document ID, frame, text selection range, scroll anchor and last focused editor. Content and persistence belong to the document, never to an app-global active buffer. Two different documents cannot share mutable content or save destinations.
- New creates a new document and primary window. Open uses standard filesystem selection; opening an already-open file activates its existing window, including when minimized. Repeated Open must not create competing editable copies. This version has one primary window per document; parallel work uses separate documents.
- Show the document name in its title and Window-menu entry; distinguish identical names by containing folder, and Untitled drafts by number. Retain native title bars, movement, close, minimize, resize, Zoom and full-screen behavior. Closing the last document leaves the app running with New, Open and Settings available.

## Persistence and exits

Autosave is enabled by default with no new disabling preference. Schedule a save after 1 second of editing inactivity and at least every 10 seconds during continuous editing; flush pending changes on app deactivation, document close and quit. These intervals are product choices, not HIG values.

| Event | Required transition |
| --- | --- |
| Edit document A | Increment A's revision and schedule only A's save. Preserve B's content, selection and persistence state. |
| Save (Command-S) | For a named document, save to its location. For Untitled, request name and location through standard Save UI, honoring extension visibility preferences; cancellation retains the draft and editor state. |
| Save completion | Clear Edited only when the persisted revision equals the current revision. A late completion for an older revision cannot clear newer edits or affect another document. |
| Save failure | Keep content and recovery data, retain Edited, and show persistent document-specific error text with Retry and Save As… access. Never present success before durable completion. |
| Close document | Finish its pending save to its file or durable draft, then record restoration state and close that window only. If persistence fails, keep the window open with recovery actions. Close does not mean discard. |
| Quit | Flush each document independently and record the open-window set. Abort quit on any unresolved save failure; retain all unsaved content. Successfully saved documents remain safe. |
| Switch window/app or minimize | Preserve content, selection and scroll; focus loss neither clears buffers nor closes windows. Background saves retain their originating document ID. |

Untitled drafts remain recoverable after close and appear in Open Recent with their distinct names. Reopening restores their content without requiring a named file. Do not remove drafts until a successful named save has durably transferred them. Explicit deletion/discard is outside this repair; no implicit discard is allowed. Named-file saving must use atomic replacement or equivalent protection so a failed write preserves the previous saved content.

Use Edited in document titles while newer changes remain unpersisted. With autosave enabled, do not add dirty dots to close controls or Window-menu names. A persisted recovery draft is durable but still Untitled; it must not imply that the user selected a file location.

## Commands and activation

Use the standard macOS menu bar and familiar keyboard equivalents:

| Surface | Command and scope |
| --- | --- |
| App menu | Settings… (Command-comma), Quit (Command-Q), app scope |
| File | New (Command-N), Open… (Command-O), Open Recent, Close (Command-W), Save (Command-S), Save As…; Save commands target the active document window |
| View | Text Size submenu: 100%, 125%, 150%, 175%, 200%; Enter/Exit Full Screen using system behavior |
| Window | Minimize (Command-M), Zoom, Bring All to Front, and open-window names; preserve normal window cycling (Command-grave) |

Text editing acts on the focused editor. Keep unavailable document commands visible and disabled when Settings is key or there is no document; they must not silently target the previously active note. Close always closes the key window. New/Open remain available from Settings and with no document windows. Preserve native key/main/inactive appearance and system layering; activation must not force all documents into the same selection or frame. No essential command depends on a bottom-edge button or toolbar visibility.

## Restoration

Persist a versioned record keyed by window ID and document ID: document file identity or draft ID, frame/display reference, selection start and length, scroll anchor, last focused editor, and open/closed status. Update after resize/move/selection changes and before close/quit. Persist content separately so view-state corruption cannot erase a document.

- Reopening an intentionally closed document restores its last view state. On relaunch with system window restoration enabled, restore only windows open at quit, preserving the last active document. Honor a system request not to reopen windows; documents and drafts remain available through Open/Recent.
- Load the correct document before applying selection and scroll. Clamp stale selection offsets to current text bounds; fall back to the document start when the anchor is invalid.

## Resizing and enlarged labels

Primary windows are freely resizable. Product starting values are a 900 × 650 pt content area, minimum 480 × 360 pt, and no app-imposed maximum below the available display size. Clamp the initial/restored frame to the visible work area; provide a compact scrollable layout if the available area is smaller than the nominal minimum. Validate these proposed dimensions on Mac before release.

Use standard macOS control fonts and semantic text roles. macOS has no Dynamic Type: provide the app-wide Text Size accommodation above, default 100%, persisting across launches and applying to app-owned reading text, labels and controls through 200%. This is display configuration; it must not change saved note text or mark documents Edited. Respect system accessibility preferences rather than duplicating them.

Measure layout from available width and scaled text. Labels wrap into growing containers; label/control rows stack vertically whenever their intrinsic widths plus spacing exceed available width. The editor fills remaining space, wraps prose and scrolls vertically. Settings content also scrolls when needed. Never shrink text to make it fit, clip essential labels, or lock row heights. Keep selection and scroll anchor through reflow, resizing and full-screen transitions. Essential actions stay reachable through menus when the lower window edge is offscreen.

## Settings window

Settings… opens one reusable auxiliary window, with no document ID or note buffer. Repeated invocation brings that window forward. For this repair it contains one General pane for app-wide defaults, including Text Size; title it “Architecture Notes Settings.” Persist valid changes immediately and restore values on reopen. Closing it changes no document content, save status or open-window record. Dim minimize/zoom as appropriate for the native settings window; size content to its pane with scrolling for enlarged text. If panes are added later, use stable noncustomizable navigation, the current pane title, and restore the last pane. Frequent document view options remain local to their document; future document configuration belongs in File.

## Release acceptance

The executable scenarios and evidence status are in result.md. Release requires independent document saves, failed-save protection, repeated-open reuse, close/reopen and relaunch restoration, key-window command routing, and usable minimum/large/full-screen layouts at 100% and 200% text with long labels. Keyboard-only and Full Keyboard Access task completion require native Mac verification.

## Guidance basis

These are product requirements informed by the installed local HIG snapshot, not API availability claims. See [Windows — macOS](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/windows#macOS), [File management — Saving work](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/file-management#Saving-work), [Settings — macOS](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/settings#macOS), [Layout — Adaptability](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/layout#Adaptability), [Typography — macOS](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/typography#macOS), [Accessibility — Vision](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/accessibility#Vision), [The menu bar](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/the-menu-bar), [Keyboards](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/keyboards), and [Multitasking — macOS](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/multitasking#macOS). Links identify sources; no network access was used.
